en: Exploring how to use your voice and body on stage will help you tackle the most important piece of giving a powerful talk: connecting with your audience.
People aren't computers. They're social creatures with all kinds of unique traits.
Your first job as a speaker is to build a trusting human bond with your audience. There are many ways to do that. Here are five suggestions:
1. Make eye contact. Make eye contact with members of your audience right from the start of your talk and continue making eye contact throughout.

Humans learn a lot about one another through eye contact. Our brains can detect the tiniest muscle movements in someone else's eyes. We use that information to figure out all sorts of things— like how that person is feeling and whether or not we can trust them. And while we’re doing that, they’re figuring out the same things about us. Scientists have even shown that when two people stare at one another, their brains start to adopt the same emotional state. So when we make eye contact, our minds link up.

2. Show vulnerability. One of the best ways to put an audience at ease is to reveal your own vulnerability. It’s like a tough cowboy walking into a saloon and opening his coat to show he's not carrying any weapons. Everyone relaxes.

Take this example from Ethan Lisi, who spoke at a TED-Ed Student Talks event in 2020. “Another common stereotype that is often associated with autism is that autistic people lack empathy. And again, this is not true. I actually have lots of empathy. I’m just not really good at showing it. Whenever a friend is trying to tell me some of the struggles that they’re going through, I often don’t know how to express my reply. And that is why I don't show as much empathy as my non-autistic friends do. Emotional expression, however much or however little, is difficult for me. And that is because I am bursting inside with every single emotion one feels at all times. Though, of course, I cannot express it that way. Otherwise, let’s say happiness, for example, would come out as a huge burst of gleeful wheezing, hand flapping, and loud vocal ‘woohoo!’ Whereas you may just smile.”

Ethan's willingness to open up about something vulnerable helps the audience open up as well; allowing them to see him, and perhaps the world, from a new perspective. We feel connected. We're ready and eager to learn more. Sharing something vulnerable is a powerful tool a speaker can use to connect to an audience. But, as with anything powerful, it should be handled with care. It is possible to share too much personal information in a talk, in a way that makes the audience feel uncomfortable. Make sure any vulnerable moments you include are there to help support the message you are trying to deliver. If they aren't doing that, it's probably best to leave them out. Vulnerability related to your message is powerful. Sharing something personal just for the sake of it is not. If you're not sure whether or not a vulnerable moment is appropriate, try your talk out on an honest friend.
3. Make them laugh, but not squirm.

Concentrating on a talk can be hard work for an audience. Humor is a wonderful way to keep everyone with you. Remember Sophie Scott’s talk from Lesson One? If Sophie is right, part of the reason laughter exists is that it helps humans form bonds. When you laugh with someone, you both feel you're on the same side. It's a fantastic tool for building a connection. Some of the very best speakers in the world spend a lot of time building this connection in their talks.

However, take caution. Spending a lot of time on funny stories, while still delivering a meaningful message, is difficult. It's not recommended for most talks. But, if you can find just one short story that makes people smile, it may unlock the rest of what you have to say.

4. Park your ego. Would you want to listen to someone who seems completely full of themselves? Nothing hurts a talk more than the sense that the speaker is showing off. If an audience gets that impression early on in a talk, look out. They will likely stop listening. TED Speaker Salman Khan put it beautifully, “Be yourself. The worst talks are the ones where someone is trying to be someone they aren’t. If you are generally goofy, then be goofy. If you are emotional, then be emotional. The one exception to that is if you are arrogant and self-centered, then you should definitely pretend to be someone else.”

Ego can show up in a lot of ways the speaker may not even be aware of, such as: name dropping, telling stories just to show off, boasting about your achievements, or making the talk all about you. Remember that the purpose of your talk is to gift an idea, not tell everyone how great you are.

Still, these things can be hard to catch yourself on. Every leader needs someone she can count on for honest feedback. Someone who's not afraid to tell her the truth about how she's coming across, even if that's difficult to hear. A good way to know whether or not your talk seems boastful is to read it for that trusted person. Give them the chance to say, “That was great in parts, but honestly, you came across a little full of yourself.”

5. Tell a story. We’re born to love stories. They create interest, empathy, emotion, and a sense of mystery. They can help an audience understand why a topic matters to you, and encourage them to care about that topic, too.

Powerful stories can be great at any stage of a talk. A great way to open, a great way to make your point in the middle, and sometimes (though less often) a great way to end. The stories that work best to connect with the audience are the stories about you personally, or about the people close to you. Tales of failure, awkwardness, bad luck, danger or disaster, when told honestly, can really hook an audience. They start really listening. They start to share some of your emotions. They start to care about you. They start to like you.
But be careful.
The stories you tell must be authentic to you. Again, stories that seem boastful will push an audience away. Ask yourself: is it the real me telling this story?

A good test is to imagine whether or not you would tell the story to a group of friends. If so, how would you tell it? Friends are good at knowing when you’re trying to be someone other than you. And so are audiences. Be yourself and you won't go wrong.

The suggestions and tools in this lesson should all be used as part of a real desire to connect to your audience. It's that connection that's important. You’re a human, and your listeners are humans. Think of them as friends and reach out with your gift.
zh: 探索如何在舞台上 用自己的声音和身体， 将有助于你完成一场 有力的演讲中最重要的部分： 与观众建立关系。
人不是计算机。 它们是具有各种独特特征的社交生物。
作为演讲者，你的第一份工作 是与听众建真实的人际关系。 有很多方法可以做到这一点。 以下是五个建议：
1. 进行眼神交流。 从演讲一开始就与听众进行眼神交流， 并在整个演讲过程中保持眼神交流。
人类可以通过眼神交流互相了解。 我们的大脑可以探测到别人 眼中最微小的肌肉运动。 我们使用这些信息 来弄清楚各种各样的事情， 例如那个人的感受 以及我们是否可以信任他们。 在我们这样做的同时， 他们对我们也是一样的。 科学家甚至表明， 当两个人互相盯着对方时， 他们的大脑开始呈现相同的情绪状态。 因此，当我们进行眼神交流时， 我们的思想就会相联。
2. 显示脆弱性。 让观众安心的最好方法之一 是揭露自己的脆弱。 这就像一个强壮的牛仔走进了个酒吧， 然后打开外套 以表明自己没有携带任何武器。 大家都放松了。

以伊桑·利西（Ethan Lisi）为例， 他在 2020 年的一次 TED-Ed 学生座谈会上发表了讲话。 “通常与自闭症相关的 另一种常见刻板印象 是自闭症患者缺乏同理心。 再说一遍，这不是真的， 其实我特别有同情心， 我只是不太擅长展示它。 每当朋友想告诉我 他们正在经历的一些困难时， 我常常不知道如何表达我的回复。 所以我不像非自闭症朋友那样 表现出强烈同情心。 情感表达，无论多么少， 对我来说都很困难。 那是因为我的内心深处充斥着 人们无时无刻感受到的每一种情绪。 但是，当然，我不能这样表达出来。 要不然，举个例子，假设幸福 会以一阵欢快的喘息、 拍手和响亮的声音 “哇哦！”的形式表现出来， 而你可能只会微笑一下。”

伊桑愿意分享一些他的脆弱， 这也有助于观众敞开心扉； 让他们，或许还有世界， 能从新的角度看待他。 我们感到彼此紧密相连。 我们已经准备好了并且想解更多。 分享自己脆弱的内容是演讲者 可以用来与观众建立联系的强大工具。 但是，与任何强大的东西一样， 应谨慎处理。 在演讲中分享过多的个人信息是可能的， 这会让听众感到不舒服。 确保你包括的任何脆弱时刻 都能支持你想要传达的信息。 若不能起到这样的作用， 那最好还是不要提。 与你要表达信息相关的脆弱非常有力。 而单纯为了分享而分享的则不然。 如果你不确定脆弱的时刻是否合适， 可以试着找一位 值得信赖的朋友听你演讲。
3. 让他们笑，但不要让他们感到不安。
对于听众来说，专注于 一个演讲可能很难。 幽默是让所有人与你同频的绝佳方式。 还记得第一课中索菲·斯科特 （Sophie Scott）的演讲吗？ 如果索菲是对的， 那么笑声之所以存在， 部分原因是它可以帮助人类建立关系。 当你和某人一起笑时， 你们俩都会觉得自己站在同一边。 这是建立关系的绝佳工具。 世界上一些最优秀的演讲者在演讲中 花费了大量时间来建立这种联系。
但是，请谨慎行事。 在传递有意义的信息的同时， 又花费大量时间在有趣的故事上， 是很困难的。 不建议在大多数演讲中使用。 但是，如果你能找到一个 能让人微笑的短篇故事， 它可能会解开你所说的其余内容。

4. 放下你的自我。 你会想听一个看上去 完全自以为是的人的话吗？ 没有什么比演讲者 炫耀的感觉更能伤演讲了。 如果听众在演讲初期有 这个印象，那就要当心了。 他们很可能会停止倾听。 TED 讲者萨尔曼·汗 （Salman Khan）说得很好： “做你自己。 最糟糕的演讲是有人想装成别人。 如果你通常很搞笑，那就搞笑起来。 如果你很情绪化，那就情绪化。 唯一的例外是，如果你 傲慢自大，以自我为中心， 那么你一定要假装自己是别人。”
自我可能以多种方式出现， 演讲者甚至可能没有意识到， 比如：提及姓名、讲故事只为了炫耀、 吹嘘自己的成就， 或者把所有话题都放在你身上。 请记住，你演讲的目的是给出一个想法， 不是告诉所有人你有多棒。
尽管如此，这些事情可能很难让自己着手。 每位领导者都需要一个可以 信赖的人来获得诚实的反馈。 一个不怕告诉她真相的人， 尽管这听着有些困难。 要知道你的演讲是否显得自夸， 一个好方法 是给那个值得信赖的人读一读。 让他们有机会说， “这在某些地方很棒，但说实话， 你表现的有点自满。”
5. 会讲故事。 我们生下来就喜欢故事。 它们创造兴趣、同理心、情感和神秘感。 它们可以帮助观众理解 为什么一个话题对你很重要， 并鼓励他们也关心这个话题。
有力的故事在演讲的任何阶段都可能很棒。 这是一种很好的开场方式，也是 一种在中间表达观点的好方法， 也有时（尽管不太常见）是结束的好方法。 最能与观众建立连接的故事 是关于你个人的故事， 或者关于你身边人的故事。 故事关于失败、尴尬、运气不好、 危险或灾难的故事，确实会吸引观众。 他们开始认真倾听。 他们开始分享你的一些情绪。 他们开始关心你。 他们开始喜欢你。
但是要小心。
你讲的故事对你来说必须是真实的。 再一次，看似夸张的故事会把观众赶走。 问问自己：是真实的我在讲这个故事吗？
一个很好的测试是想象一下 你是否会把这个故事讲 给一群朋友。 如果会，你会怎么讲呢？ 朋友们很擅长知道你 有没有在装成你以外的人。 观众也是如此。 做你自己，你不会出错。
本课中的建议和工具都应作为 真正渴望与受众建立关系的一部分， 这种关系才是重要的。 你是人类，你的听众是人类。 把他们当作朋友，并拿出你的礼物。

en: Whether you memorize a script, or read from one, or use a few notes, or don’t use any notes at all, a talk that is well-prepared and passionately delivered will always impact an audience. But what does delivering a talk passionately look like? It's time to find your voice.

Here’s a radical question: why bother to give a talk? Why not simply email the script to every potential member of the audience? One of the special things about TED is that it shows how talks can offer something more than printed words.
But that doesn’t just happen automatically. Not every talk offers something extra. That something extra has to be thought about, invested in, and developed. It has to be earned.
What is that something extra? It’s our humanity. Our humanity turns information into inspiration.

Here are some of the things the human layer can bring to a text. Connection: I trust this person. Engagement: every sentence sounds so interesting! Curiosity: I hear it in your voice and see it in your face. Understanding: the emphasis on that word with that hand gesture, now I get it. Empathy: I can tell how much that hurt you. Excitement: wow, that passion is infectious! Conviction: such determination in those eyes. Action: I want to be on your team. Sign me up!

Together, these things create inspiration. We think of inspiration as the force that tells the brain what to do with a new idea. Many ideas just get filed away, and probably soon forgotten. Inspiration, on the other hand, sets off our mind’s attention alert system.
There are two major things to consider when preparing a talk for an audience. The first is: what am I doing with my voice? And the second is: what am I doing with my body?
Speak with meaning.

Listen to the opening minute of the TED Talk by George Monbiot. “When I was a young man, I spent six years of wild adventure in the tropics, working as an investigative journalist in some of the most bewitching parts of the world. I was as reckless and foolish as only young men can be— this is why wars get fought— but I also felt more alive than I’ve ever done since. And when I came home, I found the scope of my existence gradually diminishing, until loading the dishwasher seemed like an interesting challenge. And I found myself sort of scratching at the walls of life, as if I was trying to find a way out into a wider space beyond. I was, I believe, ecologically bored.”

When you hear Monbiot speak, you find yourself pulled into his world. He uses his voice in a way that adds meaning to every word he says. That's something you wouldn't get if you read his script in a book. His words are interesting, but it’s the way he says them that gives his audience a feeling of curiosity and astonishment. How does he do this?

The key to being an exciting speaker is to create variety in the way you speak— variety based on the meaning you’re trying to get across. So many speakers forget this. They give a talk in which every sentence sounds the same, with a slight rise at the start and a drop at the end. There are no pauses or changes of pace. This communicates that no single part of a talk matters more than any other part. It’s just the same thing over and over again until the end. Listening to a talk like this can feel like being hypnotized. That is, it puts an audience to sleep.

If your talk is scripted, try this: find the most important two or three words in each sentence and underline them. Then, look for the one word in each paragraph that really matters, and underline it twice. If there are bits that are lighthearted or playful, run a wavy pencil line under those. Look for every question mark, and highlight it with a yellow highlighter. Find the single biggest “Aha” moment in the whole talk, and put a great big black blob right before it. If there's a joke or a funny story, put little pink dots above it.

Now, try reading your script, making sure to change your voice in response to each mark. For example, let yourself laugh a little while looking at the pink dots. Pause for the big black blob. And speed up a bit for the wavy pencil line, or speak more softly. How does that sound?

Now, try one more thing. Remember all the emotions associated with each section of your talk. Which bits are you most passionate about? Which issues make you angry? What makes you laugh? What confuses you? Read your talk again, letting those emotions out a little as you speak. Try doing this with a friend. See what she responds to, or what she rolls her eyes at. Record yourself reading your talk, then play it back with your eyes closed. How's it sounding?

Don’t struggle to add variety to your voice when that doesn’t feel right to you. Let it come naturally from the passion you feel for your idea. You want to sound like yourself, expressing curiosity and excitement when it's appropriate.

You know the voice you use when you’re catching up with friends or family members you haven’t seen in a while? That’s the kind of voice you’ll want to use to present your talk: real, natural, and unafraid to let it rip if what you’re saying demands it.

It’s important to use your body too. Sometimes a speaker will give the impression that his body is only there to carry his head onto the stage. Once in front of the audience, the body no longer knows what to do with itself. It stands awkwardly, hands glued to its side, or sways back and forth from one leg to the other. But there are a few things you can think about that may help you feel more comfortable on stage and make you seem more confident to your audience.

The simplest way to present a talk powerfully is just to stand tall. Put equal weight on both your feet, keeping your feet a few inches apart. Use your hands and arms to naturally emphasize whatever it is you’re saying. This is enough to signal to the audience that you’re calm and that you know what you’re talking about. This is the method used by a majority of TED speakers. The key is to feel relaxed and to let your upper body move freely. Good posture helps. Avoid slouching your shoulders forward. Standing so openly may feel vulnerable, but that vulnerability can be nice for an audience to see.

Some speakers prefer to walk the stage. It helps them think. It helps them emphasize key moments, and, this is important, they frequently stop to dwell on important points. It's that change in rhythm that makes the walking method work. Constant pacing without a change in rhythm can be tiring to watch. But pacing broken up by moments of stillness can be powerful.

Something to avoid is nervously shifting from leg to leg, or walking forward and back a couple of steps, in a kind of rocking motion. Many speakers do this without realizing it. They may be feeling a little anxious, and shifting from one leg to the other eases their discomfort. But, from the audience’s point of view, it actually highlights that discomfort.

The difference between a speaker who rocks back and forth and a speaker who finds stillness can be huge for an audience. So, move if you want to, but only move if you can move with purpose. Then, when you want to emphasize a point, stop moving and address your audience from a stance of calm power.

There are plenty of other ways you can speak with power too. Dame Stephanie Shirley chose to sit for her talk, using a metal stool with one foot tucked back on a rung, and notes in her lap. It looked relaxed and natural. The late, great neurologist Oliver Sacks also sat for his talk. Clifford Stoll leapt and darted around the stage with such energy, it added an entirely new and unique flavor to his talk. So there are no rules. You just have to find a way of being on stage that makes you feel comfortable and confident, and that doesn’t distract from what you’re saying.

The simple test is to rehearse in front of a small audience, and ask them if your body language is getting in the way of your message. Or, record yourself speaking and watch it back to see if you’re doing anything you didn’t know you were doing with your body.

There's a place in the world for all types of presentation styles. Just make sure your body knows it’s not just there to carry your head around. It's allowed to enjoy its time on stage. Do it your way. Don't try to be someone else. Focus on your idea and your passion for it. And don't be afraid to let your own personality shine through.
zh: 无论是提前背稿、照稿朗读、 借助提示还是直接脱稿， 只要准备充分且演讲时饱含激情， 你总能打动观众。 但饱含激情的演讲到底是什么样的？ 是时候找到独属于你的表达方式了。
但首先，我们得回答一个尖锐的问题： 为什么非得演讲呢？ 直接把讲稿群发给所有潜在观众 不是更省事吗？ TED 的一大独特价值就在于， 它证明了演讲有着超越文字的力量。
但这种力量并不会凭空产生， 也并非每场演讲都具有。 我们得精心构思、 倾情投入和反复打磨， 以实实在在的努力获得这种力量。
不过这种力量究竟是什么呢？ 它是人性蕴含的温度。 这份温度能将信息转化为灵感。
以下是人性的温度 能为文本注入的额外价值： 联结：我信任这个人。 投入：每句话听着都好有意思！ 好奇：我从你的语气 和表情里感受到了。 理解：特意强调这个词， 再加上这种手势， 现在我懂了！ 共情：我能感受到这件事 对你的伤害有多大。 兴奋：哇！好有感染力！ 信念：多么坚定的眼神！ 行动：我想加入。算我一个！
以上因素相互交织，共同催生出灵感。 我们不妨将灵感视作一种精神指引， 它会告诉大脑该拿新想法怎么办。 许多想法都会被大脑收集归档， 然后大概率被快速遗忘。 但灵感却能 引起大脑警觉。
在准备演讲时， 主要得考虑以下两个问题： 第一：如何运用声音？ 第二：如何调动肢体？
用声音传递意义。

下面请听乔治·蒙比奥的 TED 演讲开场部分： “我年轻的时候 是个调查记者， 在热带地区野外探险了六年， 探索了世界上不少极具魅力的地方。 那个时候的我鲁莽又愚蠢。 事实上，这种年轻人独有的特质 也是战争的根源， 但我也感觉自己的生命 前所未有地鲜活。 回国之后， 我感觉自己生活的天地在慢慢变小， 到最后连怎么摆洗碗机里的盘子 都成了件挺有挑战性的趣事。 我感觉自己有点像在抓挠生活的墙， 想找到条路，去开阔点的地方。 我觉得自己患上了生态性无聊症。”
听着蒙比奥的讲述， 你不知不觉就被拉进了他的世界。 他用声音为每个字赋予了新的内涵， 这是阅读文字稿无法感受到的。 他的讲稿确实很有趣， 但真正让观众产生好奇与惊叹的， 其实是他的讲述方式。 但他是怎么做到的？
优秀的演讲者懂得根据内容 调整自己的讲述方式。 但太多的演讲者忘记了这一点。 在他们的演讲里， 每句话听起来都一样： 开头语调略微上扬，结尾下降。 没有停顿，也没有节奏变化。 这等于在告诉观众： 每个部分都差不多， 没有哪里特别重要。 整个演讲从头到尾一模一样， 直到结束。 这种演讲听着就像是催眠， 让人昏昏欲睡。
如果你手上有稿子，可以试着这么做： 找到每句话里最重要的两三个词， 用下划线标出来。 然后再找到每个段落里 最重要的那个词， 用双下划线标出来。 轻松幽默的内容 用波浪线划出。 找到问句就用 黄色荧光笔高亮标记。 找到整个演讲里最大的爆点， 在前面画个黑色实心圆点。 笑话或趣闻上方点粉色小点。
现在再试着读一遍你的讲稿， 记得一定要根据标记调整声音。 比如，看到粉色小点声音里带点笑， 看到黑色实心圆点时停顿一下， 看到波浪线时稍稍加速， 或把声音放轻一点。 现在听起来如何？
下面再试着做另一件事： 回忆演讲里每个片段对应的情绪。 哪些部分最让你激动？ 哪些议题让你愤怒？ 什么让你发笑？ 什么让你困惑？ 再读一遍你的讲稿， 让这些情绪自然流露出来。 你可以找个朋友演练一下， 看看哪些地方能引发她的共鸣， 哪些让她忍不住翻白眼。 你也可以把自己读讲稿的过程录下来， 然后闭上眼睛回放听听。 听起来是什么感觉？
如果某种声音变化让你觉得别扭， 就不要硬加。 尝试让变化从你对自己的想法 抱有的热情中自然产生。 你得做你自己， 在该好奇时好奇，该兴奋时兴奋。
还记得你跟好久不见的亲友 是怎么说话的吗？ 就用这种方式演讲： 真实自然，该放开时放开。
肢体动作也很重要。 有些演讲者让人感觉， 他们的身体除了把脑袋带上舞台之外 没有其他作用。 一面对观众， 他们就不知道该怎么动了， 就只是僵硬地站着，双手紧贴大腿， 或者不自在地左右晃动。 不过有些方法能让你 在台上更自在， 也能让观众觉得你更自信。
最简单的一个是站直。 双脚稍微分开，平摊身体重量。 用自然的手部动作强调说话内容。 这样观众就能看出你很从容， 对自己讲的内容很有把握。 大多数 TED 演讲者都会用这种方法。 关键在于放松身体， 让上半身的动作舒展自然。 良好的体态对演讲也有帮助。 不要含胸驼背。 这种不设防的站姿可能会让你 感觉没有安全感， 但观众会感受到你的坦诚。
有些演讲者喜欢在舞台上走动。 这能帮助他们思考， 也让他们能更好地强调关键内容。 更重要的一点是， 他们可以时常停下， 然后深入阐述要点。 走动式演讲的效果就来源于 这种节奏变化。 持续不断的走动会让观众疲劳， 但动静结合的步调却充满力量。
不过一定不要紧张地频繁更换支撑脚， 或者像钟摆一样， 小范围来回踱步。 很多演讲者会下意识这么做。 他们可能有点紧张， 而改变身体重心能缓解这种情绪。 但在观众眼里这种情绪 反而更明显了。
摇摆不定与沉稳静止的演讲者 给观众的观感差异巨大。 总之，走动是可以的， 但一定不要随便乱动。 等到需要强调重点时， 停下脚步，以沉稳的姿态面对观众。
除此之外，还有很多 能为演讲增添力量的方法。 史蒂芬妮·雪莉女士选择坐着演讲， 一只脚搭在金属凳的横杠上， 笔记放在膝盖上。 看起来放松又自然。 已故的著名神经学家奥利弗·萨克斯 也选择坐着演讲。 克利福德·斯托尔则在台上 活力满满地跳跃穿梭， 为演讲注入独特韵味。 所以演讲没有既定规则。 你只需要找到一种 让自己感觉舒适自信的演讲方式， 并且确保它不会干扰观众 接收演讲内容。
一个简单的检验方法是 找点观众小范围试讲， 然后问问他们有没有 被你的肢体动作干扰。 或者你也可以自己录视频回看， 看看有没有下意识的小动作。
不同的演讲风格都有其存在的价值。 你只需要记住：你的身体不只是用来 搬运脑袋的。 它也有权享受舞台上的时光。 用你自己的方式演讲， 无需模仿别人。 专注于呈现独属于你的想法和热情。 别害怕展现真实的自己。

en: Your first job as a speaker is to build a trusting human bond with your audience.
One excellent way to connect to an audience is to tell a story.
Stories helped make us who we are. Really — evidence left behind from our ancient ancestors suggests that the human mind developed alongside human storytelling.

Fire created a new magnet for bonding. Its warmth and flickering light drew people together after dark. This seems to have happened in every ancient culture over the last 300,000 years. And what did our ancestors do with this time together? In many cultures, one type of communal activity became very important: storytelling. Stories brought people from faraway places to the fireside. Stories about people who were alive and people who were dead, nearby and in distant lands. Stories sparked laughter, tension, and amazement.

Stories also played an important role in helping expand people’s ability to imagine and to dream, and to understand the minds of others. Storytellers became important people within a community, and their listeners took information from the stories that changed how they behaved in the world.
It's not just that we all love hearing stories. Stories probably helped shape how our minds share and receive information. So it's no surprise that many of the best talks are built around a story.

The most basic way of breaking down a story is this: a character with a goal meets an unexpected obstacle. She tries to overcome that obstacle, which builds to a peak in the action. Finally, there’s some kind of resolution to the conflict.
When it comes to sharing a story from the stage, remember four key things:
1. Base the story around a character your audience can empathize with.
2. Build tension, either through curiosity, relationship with other characters, or actual danger.
3. Offer the right level of detail. If there's not enough, the story won't come to life. If there's too much, it will get bogged down.
And, 4. End with a satisfying conclusion, whether it’s funny, moving, or surprising.

Some great talks are built around a single story. This can be really helpful for a speaker. The throughline is simply the plot of the story. If the story is about you, it can even create empathy in the audience. If your journey is exciting and easy to follow, this type of talk can work really well. But there's a trap here too.

Remember, the goal is to give. Personal stories may entertain or interest an audience, or make the speaker feel really good about themselves, but they don’t necessarily give the audience something they can walk away with; a new way of understanding things, actionable information, context, hope. And that’s a real shame.

The key is to link together the important moments of your story in a way that can be meaningful to someone else. Otherwise, it may sound like you're just rambling or speaking for the sake of hearing yourself talk.

But, if the journey reveals something powerful you have learned, and if each step in your journey is revealed with humility and honesty and vulnerability, it is a journey we will gladly take with you.

There is one other piece that is absolutely essential if you’re going to tell your own story: it has to be true. This may seem obvious, but sometimes speakers are tempted to exaggerate or even make a story up entirely. Stories can have such a big impact that some speakers are tempted to bend the truth. But even small exaggerations can quickly destroy your reputation. It's not worth the risk.

When you combine a truthful story with a desire to benefit others, you can give your listeners an extraordinary gift. A story can affect people deeply. Use it, and you can greatly increase your connection with an audience. But please, let it mean something.

What if you need someone to understand an idea that's difficult to explain? Explaining a complicated idea so that someone can understand it is one of the ways society moves forward. Harvard psychologist Dan Gilbert came to TED with a difficult task. In just a single short talk, he planned to explain a complicated concept called “Synthesized Happiness,” and why it leads us to make incorrect predictions about our own futures. Let's see how he goes about his task.

When you have 21 minutes to speak, 2 million years seems like a really long time. But evolutionarily, 2 million years is nothing. And yet in 2 million years, the human brain has nearly tripled in mass; going from the one and a quarter pound brain of our ancestor here, Habilis, to the almost 3 pound meatloaf that everybody here has between their ears. What is it about a big brain that nature was so eager for every one of us to have one?
Do you feel a little spark of curiosity? That's the first step to a successful explanation. Once a mind is curious, it opens up. Gilbert continues to spark our curiosity.

Well, it turns out when brains triple in size, they don't just get three times bigger, they gain new structures. And one of the main reasons that our brain got so big is because it got a new part called the frontal lobe— and particularly a part called the prefrontal cortex. Now, what does a prefrontal cortex do for you that should justify the entire architectural overhaul of the human skull in the blink of evolutionary time?
While keeping us interested, Gilbert introduced the first concept he’ll be building on: prefrontal cortex.

Turns out the prefrontal cortex does lots of things. But one of the most important things it does is an experience simulator. Pilots practice in flight simulators so that they don't make real mistakes in planes. Human beings have this marvelous adaptation that they can actually have experiences in their heads before they try them out in real life. This is a trick that none of our ancestors could do, that no other animal can do quite like we can. It's a marvelous adaptation. It’s up there with opposable thumbs and standing upright and language as one of the things that got our species out of the trees and into the shopping mall.

Gilbert just slipped in a second new concept: experience simulator. That’s another key building block in the big idea he’s planning to explain. The metaphor— that of a flight simulator— helps us understand what an experience simulator is. Now how about an example?

All of you have done this. I mean, you know, Ben & Jerry’s doesn’t have liver and onion ice cream, and it’s not because they whipped some up, tried it, and went yuck! It’s because, without leaving your armchair, you can simulate that flavor and say yuck before you make it.
Gilbert uses a single strong example of how the experience simulator works, and then you totally get what it is. But now the talk takes a turn.

Gilbert asks the audience to use their experience simulators to imagine going through two very different life events: winning the lottery and becoming paraplegic— which means losing the use of your legs. He asks everyone which of these life events they would prefer to happen to them. Then he shares a truly amazing piece of information.

Interestingly, there are data on these two groups of people, data on how happy they are. And this is exactly what you expected, isn't it? But these aren’t the data, I made these up. These are the data. You failed the pop quiz, and you’re hardly five minutes into the lecture. Because the fact is that a year after losing the use of their legs and a year after winning the lotto, lottery winners and paraplegics are equally happy with their lives.

What? That can't be right. This new concept of the experience simulator has suddenly taken you to a place you didn't expect. A confusing place. You’re in what’s called a knowledge gap. There’s more information you need in order to understand the facts Gilbert has just presented to you. He goes on to fill in that gap.

He and his coworkers have been researching something called impact bias, which is the tendency for our experience simulators to work badly— to make us believe different experiences are more different than they actually are.

By putting a name on it, impact bias, the mystery of the information we’re struggling to make sense of starts to become more believable. Our curiosity is now burning more brightly than before. Gilbert uses our curiosity to reveal the big idea of his talk.

In fact, they really are, from field studies to laboratory studies, we see that winning or losing an election, gaining or losing a romantic partner, getting or not getting a promotion, passing or not passing a college test, on and on, have far less impact, less intensity, and much less duration than people expect them to have. Now, in fact, a recent study— this almost floors me— a recent study showing how major life traumas affect people suggests that if it happened over three months ago, with only a few exceptions, it has no impact whatsoever on your happiness.

Why? Because happiness can be synthesized. Sir Thomas Brown wrote in 1642, “I am the happiest man alive. I have that in me that can convert poverty to riches, adversity to prosperity, I am more invulnerable than Achilles; fortune hath not one place to hit me.” Kind of remarkable machinery does this guy have in his head? Well, it turns out it’s precisely the same remarkable machinery that all of us have. Human beings have something that we might think of as a psychological immune system, a system of cognitive processes, largely non-conscious cognitive processes, that help them change their views of the world so that they can feel better about the worlds in which they find themselves.

There it is, Gilbert’s big idea: something called Synthetic Happiness. He goes on to describe how this works. It's like an immune system for the mind. Just as the immune system protects our bodies from infection, synthesized happiness protects our peace of mind. Our brains build happiness for themselves, even when things don’t go as planned. Gilbert got his audience to understand synthesized happiness by building on the concepts of prefrontal cortex, experience simulator, and impact bias. And to make it clear, he used another metaphor: the immune system. Gilbert didn’t try to explain his complicated idea in one big leap. He got there piece by piece. After giving us some examples of synthesized happiness in action, He goes on to show how you can live a wiser, happier life if you remember synthetic happiness exists. At the end of the explanation, the way we see the world has been upgraded. It’s richer, deeper, and truer.

There is a lot of evidence out there suggesting that this is how understanding must be built. Like a tower, each new block of information supports the next new block of information. Each bit gets stronger thanks to metaphors and examples. The metaphors show us the shape of each new idea so that the mind knows how to recognize it.

If the core of your talk is explaining a powerful new idea, it’s helpful to ask: what do you think your audience already knows? What are the building blocks you need to explain your idea? What metaphors and examples can you use to help listeners understand things they may not be familiar with yet?

It can be tricky to spot what things an audience may need help understanding. We all suffer from something economist Robin Hogarth calls “the curse of knowledge.” Basically, we find it hard to remember what it feels like not to know something that we ourselves do know. This might be the most important requirement for clear communication.
You can’t give a powerful new idea to an audience unless you can figure out how to explain it. That can only be done step by step, fueled by curiosity.
My name is Yinka Ilory, an artist, designer, a storyteller, a dreamer, and a person who loves color. I believe that my calling and mission is to bring joy to the world.

We live in a time where everyone's asking the same question: "Who am I and what brings me joy?" Looking back now, I realize this question has followed me my whole life. While joy was always present in my life and always around me, I just didn't have the language for it. But what I did have was a world rich of color, symbols, dreams and affirmation.

I grew up in London in 27 Ashby House, on a council estate. I was raised by Nigerian parents who moved to London in the 1980s. My mother from Ondo State, coined the Sunshine State. It's known for its majestic rock landscapes and warm weather. The people there are warm, grounded and strong.

My father from Ekiti State in southwest Nigeria, a place known for its nature and famous for its warm and cold springs, a place called Ikogosi, and known as the Fountain of Knowledge because of its reputation for academic excellence and intellectual achievement. Even before I'd been to these places, I could picture myself growing up there, being raised there. But I was born and raised in London. I felt a strong sense of connection and a strong sense of belonging to a place I'd call home.

In the UK, my beloved mother did many things. She bought and sold Swiss voile lace. She catered for weddings and birthdays. She was an architect of joy, architect of bringing people and things together. In our glass cabinet at home, she would collect objects of memories she treasured in her show glass.
My dad worked in retail. Everyone called him Uncle Paul. He was everyone's uncle, dad, brother, mentor and therapist. He brought so much joy to the workplace.

At one point, my parents also owned a corner shop in London. It was insane. We had all the kids after school, people in the estate, the neighbors, passersby would come to the corner shop. This place became a gathering point for the whole community. On Sundays, my mum and dad would host church services. They would lead lectures and sermons. The words of worship and affirmation, singing and moving have manifested in my memory. My parents loved house parties, live music, plates of jollof rice weaving in our small council flat. Different languages. Different journeys. All in one room. My parents brought all these rituals of community and faith and pleasure with them from Nigeria to the UK. As a child, I didn't realize I was experiencing a daily baptism of joy, a joy that had been passed on from generation to generation without even knowing it. Every ritual, every gathering, every exchange carried a deeply symbolic meaning. All these were seeds of joy.

How did I harvest joy? Myself, I developed, like my mother, the same collective spirit. She collected objects. I collected symbols. A sun, a rock, hands, a star, a talking drum. At first I didn't know why I was drawn to these symbols, but I realized these symbols were memories or things I enjoyed and things that brought me joy as a youth. The Ondo sunlight, the rituals, the community. The gatherings. Visualizing them helps me harvest joy. Visual storytelling is how we unlock stories we already carry.

This is what I do with my work. I don't invent stories. I uncover them. I reimagine them through my lens, similar to how I reflect on my personal experiences. I listened to people's stories and experiences and turn them into symbolic symbols. Because when you visualize something, when you share it, you can pass it on to someone else, another generation. This is why I think joy is transgenerational. We can inherit it from what it was before or what surrounds us.

This is what I did in a recent experiment. I asked my Instagram audience, what does joy look like for you today? And what are your early memories of joy looking like to you today? And how could they be translated into symbols that connect with your memories? Receiving an abundance of responses felt like I was receiving another daily baptism of joy, just like my parents' rituals. I selected some of the answers and turned them into symbols. A mushroom, a cashew tree, a sports car, a palm wine cup, and I paired them up with symbols from my archive. Ripples of laughter. Precious joy. Connection, sunrise and community. This selection was based on what happened the most.

Around 80 percent of the responses carried a sense of togetherness through connection: shared, inherited, not individual. Around 65 percent of responses were connected to nature: plants, sunlight, open space, feeling through light, texture and smell. About half of the responses spoke about freedom, movement, exploration, anticipation, no restrictions. Some were talking about growth not always being immediate. Sometimes it was over time, sometimes through struggle. A small number spoke about stillness. So I took all of these impressions and turned them into an artwork, an artwork that celebrates the power of transgenerational joy. When it comes together, this is the magic you can create. But what stood out to me the most was that no one spoke about personal achievement. It was always about people and places, and shared experiences. All of my responses were very visual already. It's something we often recognize in hindsight.

To me, harvesting transgenerational joy means finding the seeds that were planted before you, by your parents, by your loved ones, by your community, even by your younger self. We all carry those seeds. To be able to see them, we need to visualize them. We harvest them by sharing them.

My parents always said to me, whatever you sow is what you shall reap. I hope today you will reap joy. Pass it on from person to person, from generation to generation. It was passed on to me and now I want to pass it on to you.
Thank you.
(Applause)

Troy’s princess, Cassandra, wasn’t cruel to her soon-to-be sister-in-law, the legendary beauty Helen, out of spite. It was because she was suffering under the weight of a tortuously twisted curse, which haunted her with appalling visions linked to Helen’s arrival.

Helen was already married to the Spartan king Menelaus, after all. And when Cassandra’s brother, Prince Paris, prepared to sail to Sparta, she foresaw his calamitous attachment to Helen and begged him to stay. But he’d merely dismissed her, fallen for Helen, and returned to Troy with her in tow. Beset by violent premonitions, Cassandra then warned that Menelaus’ vengeful crusade would lead to the brutal fall of their family and the city of Troy. But once again, people ignored her.

In fact, they always did. And this was the crux of her curse. As a young woman she had been pursued by the god Apollo. He offered her the gift of prophecy. But when she withdrew from his advances, he twisted his gift into a maddening hex: from that day on, Cassandra would be able to precisely see and describe the future— but her prophecies would never be believed. Despite this, Cassandra resolved to always speak the truth, even as her family fell deeper into denial.

Her dire warnings became increasingly repellent to her father, Trojan King Priam. And when the war began, as she’d predicted, he declared that her meddling was bad for morale and confined her to a high tower. From this unobstructed lookout, Cassandra watched everything unfold. Over 10 agonizing years, she witnessed her own grisly visions of senseless destruction come to pass on the battlefield below.

When dawn broke one day to reveal a huge wooden horse in place of the Greek encampment, the Trojans believed that the victory had finally been secured. Their enemies appeared to have fled, leaving this inscrutable token of peace behind. But as others streamed into the streets to celebrate, Cassandra realized the insidious truth.

Brandishing a battle-axe and a flaming torch, she descended from the tower and ran at the wooden horse, alerting everyone that it was a trick. Instead of heeding Cassandra’s warnings, they wrestled her to the ground and scoffed that she was getting more paranoid with age, then proceeded to tug the behemoth gift horse inside the city’s walls.

As Troy fell into an oblivious slumber that night, Greek soldiers descended from the wooden horse's belly. All had gone according to plan, and they scattered among the city streets, intoxicated with their victory, to unleash a torrent of pent up, violent chaos.

Cassandra had seen her city burn and heard her people’s screams many times, but that didn't make the reality any easier to bear. Her nightmare had come to pass. As dawn neared, the commander of the Greek army, Agamemnon himself, arrived to claim Cassandra as his prize. He dragged her back to his ship, boasting relentlessly of his victory as they set sail. But Cassandra told him plainly that he'd be punished. Earlier in the years of battle, Agamemnon had sacrificed his daughter to the war effort, hoping the gods would favor the Greeks in return. Now Cassandra saw that his wife, Clytemnestra, awaited his return, poised for revenge. But just as certainly as she saw that Agamemnon was sailing towards his own murder, Cassandra saw that she would also be killed in the fallout.

As always, she confronted the grim fate. In her lonely pact with the truth, no matter how ugly, Cassandra had always stood apart. After all, was it not her but everyone else who had fallen victim to the curse, living in deceit’s shadow, oblivious to reality until the bitter end?
zh: 特洛伊的公主卡珊德拉对即将成为她妯娌 的绝世美女海伦的刻薄并非出于恶意， 而是因为她正承受着扭曲的诅咒的重压。 这场诅咒使她被与海伦的到来 有关的骇人听闻的预卜笼罩。
毕竟，海伦已经和斯巴达国王 梅内劳斯结婚了。 当卡桑德拉的兄弟，巴黎王子 准备航行到斯巴达时， 她预见了他对海伦的灾难性依恋， 并恳求他留下来。 但是他只是忽略了她， 爱上了海伦，然后带着她回到了特洛伊。 在暴力预感的困扰下， 卡桑德拉随后警告说， 梅内劳斯的复仇十字军东征 将导致他们的家人和特洛伊市惨败。 但是，人们再次忽视了她。
实际上，他们一直如此。 这是她诅咒的症结所在。 年轻时，她曾被阿波罗神追求。 他赐予了她预言的能力作为礼物。 然而，当她退缩并拒绝他的追求时， 他把送出的礼物转换成令人发狂的咒语。 从那天起，卡桑德拉将能够 精确地预知和描述未来， 但她的预言永远不会被他人相信。 尽管如此，卡桑德拉还是决心永远说实话 哪怕面对她家人更加坚定的否认。
她那些严厉警告让她的父亲 特洛伊国王普里阿摩斯 越来越感到厌恶。 正如她所预料的那样，战争开始了， 而他却在那时宣称她的干预不利于士气， 并将她囚禁在高塔里。 在这个畅通无阻的瞭望台上， 卡桑德拉目睹了一切的发生。 在 10 年的痛苦中， 她亲眼目睹了自己对这场 愚蠢的毁灭的可怕愿景 在下面的战场上实现。
有一天黎明来临， 特洛伊人发现 一匹巨大的木马取代了 希腊的营地，特洛伊人 认为他们终于拿下了胜利。 他们的敌人似乎已经逃跑， 把这种难以理解的和平象征留给了他们。 但是，当其他人涌上街头庆祝时， 卡桑德拉意识到了这个阴险的真相。
她挥舞着一把战斧和一把燃烧的火把， 从塔上下来，冲向那匹木马， 提醒所有人这是个把戏。 他们没有听从卡桑德拉的警告， 而是把她摔倒在地， 嘲笑她随着年龄的增长变得越来越偏执， 然后开始将这匹庞然大物 的礼品马拖入城墙。
那天晚上，当特洛伊 睡的很沉时， 希腊士兵从木马的腹部爬了下来。 一切都按计划进行， 他们分散在城市街道上， 沉醉于他们的胜利， 引发了一股释放压抑的暴力混乱。

卡桑德拉亲眼目睹了她的城市被烧毁， 也多次听到她的人民的尖叫声， 但这并没有让现实变得更容易忍受。 她的噩梦成真了。 黎明临近时，希腊军队指挥官 阿伽门农本人赶来 带走卡桑德拉作为奖品。 他把她拖回自己的船上， 在他们启航时不停地吹嘘自己的胜利。 但是卡桑德拉直言不讳地 告诉他，他会受到惩罚。 在战斗的早期， 阿伽门农曾在战争中献祭了自己的女儿， 希望众神会偏爱希腊人作为回报。 现在，卡桑德拉看到他的妻子 克莱门内斯特拉正在等待他的归来， 蓄势待发准备复仇。 但是，正如她看到阿伽门农 正朝着谋杀自己的方向前进一样， 卡桑德拉看到自己也将在后果中丧生。
与往常一样，她面临着严峻的命运。 在她与真相的孤独协议中， 无论多么丑陋， 卡桑德拉始终与众不同。 毕竟，难道不是她而是其他所有 成为诅咒受害者的人 才是那生活在欺骗的阴影下， 直到痛苦的结局还对现实 一无所知的人吗？

en: A few months ago, 180 of us came together to build something in Singapore: a library. In a city where we're lucky enough to already have a world-class, highly innovative, much beloved public library system, of which I am a happy beneficiary, how is our library different? So this is a picture of the library we built. We are nestled in the heartlands of Singapore, where we sit between a 50-year-old furniture store and an antique shop, surrounded by birds and trees and ... Quite a few chickens.
(Laughter)

So our library is what we call a shared library. There are 180 shelves in our library, each of them rented and maintained by a different person. For 45 Singapore dollars a month you get to become a bookshelf owner. Being a bookshelf owner is actually really fun, because you get to share your favorite books on your own shelf, you get to decorate your own space and change up your books every now and then. Every shelf in our library is like a little pocket universe, an interesting, almost voyeuristic glimpse into someone's heart and mind. And if you walk around our library, quite often you end up standing in front of a shelf thinking to yourself, "I think I know this person," even though, strangely, you've never met this person in your entire life.

The other interesting thing about our library is that we are entirely volunteer-run. So a roster of about 40 very kind volunteer librarians take turns to keep our library open six days a week, 12 hours a day. Some of them are bookshop owners, they have a shelf in our library. Some of them are people from the community who really want to be part of the project. They are doctors, ex-lawyers, students, mothers, freelancers, retirees. We even have a five-year-old librarian among us. But we all have something in common. We love books, we believe in the power of books, and we enjoy being surrounded by books. So any time we’re open, anyone is welcome to come in, to sit down, to read a book for free, to make a friend or connection, to drink a cup of coffee, randomly brewed by someone in the library, and to just let the stress of life melt off their shoulders.

So how did we come to build a library like this? So in April this year, I took a break from my work as a photographer, and I went to Japan for a sabbatical, where I stumbled upon a small, shared community library with a similar concept. I loved it. I loved it. There was just something about the space that really enticed me. Standing in that little library in Japan, even though I couldn't read any of the Japanese books, I could sense a very powerful energy of love and care. And even though I couldn't read any of the Japanese books there, I thought it would be wonderful if we could have something like this in Singapore. So I decided to turn to social media. So I came back to Singapore, decided to write a simple Instagram post, just outlining my vision of what I thought a small, shared library in Singapore could look like. I thought if no one responded, then I would just forget about the whole thing. But if I could somehow get 50 people on board, I would be happy to give this very impractical, dreamy and idealistic idea a try. So I quickly finished writing, pressed post, and then I went back to work. By the end of the first day, I had received about 300 direct messages from people who said they were seriously interested in putting money down to rent a shelf and to build a library together. I was quite emotional that night because I could really sense people's passion and fire in their messages. Living in Singapore, where, you know, life is practical and pragmatic, this felt almost like a jailbreak kind of moment, and I think a lot of people were just waiting for the right time and the right chance to do something like this together.

I guess I was also really moved by the realization that so many people cared about books. So I took a leap of faith. I found a space to rent on the third day of the Instagram post. I signed the lease on the fourth day. I'm an Aquarius, so.
(Laughter)
With the help of many people, most of them strangers, we built the library in three months. This is a picture of us literally building the library. Here, we were installing the flooring together.

So who are some of these 180 crazy people who decided to do this with me? So this is Raymond's shelf. Raymond loves collecting CDs and books about Japan -- so these are the two things that you can find on his shelf. Every Tuesday, Raymond sets up a little stall outside our library where he sells his secondhand CDs and books. He also brews coffee -- pay as you wish -- for anyone who happens to drop by. This is Wanqi and Liam, the mother and son. Liam is also the five-year-old librarian I was talking about earlier. So far, we've been quite impressed by his work ethic.
(Laughter)

And their shelf is split half-half, half between Liam's favorite children's books, and half between Wanqi's books. Liam was also responsible for decorating their shelf. It looks great. So this particular bookshelf owner, she has decided to share some of the books that used to be on the shelves of Kin San, which is a Hong Kong bookshop that has unfortunately closed. She has also replicated a miniature version of the banner that used to hang in front of Kin San that says "ideas are bulletproof." In a way, Kin San lives on right here inside our library.

This particular bookshop owner, her name is Mira, is a preschool teacher. She believes in the power of letter writing, especially with children, which is why you can find a mailbox on her shelf. So apart from reading the amazing selection of books on her shelf, you can also write her a letter. She has promised that she'll definitely write you back.

So one of the most frequent questions we get asked is how does this library stay open? It doesn't really make economic sense, right? I think the simple answer is because 180 people have decided that it is possible to come together to build a ground-up book space for the local community. And as it turns out, this is actually quite a practical solution because this means that we're able to share the rent among 180 people, and no one person has to bear the financial burden of keeping this space open.

The other question we get asked a lot is, what do you get out of doing this? Well, we definitely don't get paid in the traditional sense, in dollars and cents. But we have been open for about four months now, and a lot of us have found the library to be one of the rare places where we feel truly at home. On most days, our library also doubles as a community center. So apart from the usual book clubs, women sharing circles, people have also used it to host curry night, hot pot night for 40 people. And also, two times a month we run a midnight library where we open till late, or at least as late as the last person would like to stay.

I see community in every corner of our little library. I see community in the people who bring food and drinks and ideas and resources to our library that they freely share with each other. People rush to return their library books even though we have no late fees -- I think because they can sense the love and the care that has gone into every shelf in our library, and also because I think they just really want to share the books with other people, right? They want other people to have access to the books. I see community in the little children who come into our library. Little kids who actually remind each other to, you know, like, please take care of the books, don't bend the pages, put the book back in the right place. I see community in our volunteer librarians, who spend a lot of time cleaning the library, cataloging books, and pouring their soul into making sure that the library is a welcoming space for everyone. And because of all this, Singapore feels a little different to me these days. These days, Singapore feels a little more generous, warm, open, kind, joyful and trusting.

In a world where people feel increasingly lonely, society feels increasingly fragmented, this little library has given us -- or at least it has given me -- a feeling of power. Not the kind of power that is heavy and destructive, but the kind of power that is light and regenerative. This little library has given me renewed hope that we do have the power to come together to build what we think is missing in our lives, in our city, in our world. And sometimes, that missing thing is a small, shared, community-owned library.
Thank you.

Joshua Johnson: Going through life with a willingness to ask more questions than you make statements? Liberating. Nothing that happens after the question is your responsibility. Your responsibility is to have the curiosity, the integrity, the thoughtfulness, and the humility to ask what's on your mind and not bite your tongue because, well, it might be uncomfortable, well, what are they going to say? Let that be their problem.
[Intersections]
[Joshua Johnson, Journalist]
[Blake Mycoskie, Social entrepreneur]
JJ: What if we shuffle the deck?
BM: I'm fine with that.
JJ: Alright. OK, deck duly shuffled.
BM: OK, you go first now.
JJ: Alright, so I can own what I've done?
BM: Yeah, yeah, exactly.
JJ: Alright, first question. Are we losing the ability to have real conversations?

BM: Hmm. I don't think so, actually. I think that with everything that's going on from a technical perspective, we are, at least in my friend group, I'm finding that people are yearning for more and more intimacy, vulnerability, you know, dinner parties, like, I'm feeling a pendulum shift back because I feel like people have been so digitally focused for so long. And no, I don't feel that way at all.

JJ: I get that, and I think the pendulum is definitely shifting. I guess when I read this, the editor in me is like, well, what do you mean by real? So I think for some folks, just being able to text you when they’re freaking out and just have that little human conversation is real connectivity because it sort of paves the way for a more open conversation. Some people aren’t ready to have the eye-to-eye, face-to-face like, conversation, but they could chat you up all day on WhatsApp and that's about as real as they can get. And I don't know, but I suspect some people kind of need to be walked from digital and virtual into real world, into real space, real time. And maybe that's what's a "real" conversation for them. It kind of pulls them towards something else.

BM: Yeah, and I also, I was just thinking, I’m probably more exposed to that because most of the work I do is in mental health now. And so most of the people I’m talking to, it’s about their mental health and their opening up about their mental health journeys. And so I'm kind of predisposed to a lot of very vulnerable, very honest, very raw conversations, probably more than the general population.
JJ: I imagine that some people start to have those conversations, their capacity for it grows and maybe their desire for it. Like, once you get the benefit of like, oh, that's what that was, then --
BM: You want more of it.
JJ: You want more of it, and you find the facility with it. For liability purposes, I'm going to start with a gentle swish and flick.
BM: OK, this is good. So many men feel lonelier than ever and don't know how to talk to one another. Where do they start?

JJ: I think that they might have to start inward, because if you're not comfortable saying, "Hey man, I'm not sure how to connect to other people," that's a level of exposure I'm not sure some guys are ready for, if you're already struggling to connect to other people. I think for some men, maybe that first conversation needs to be in the mirror And be like, "Look, this is what my life is, there's no use kidding myself. Here's where I really am. This is what's happening, this is what my social life is like, this is what my romantic life is like, this is how I see myself, this is what I actually want." And figure out if I had more connection, what would that mean to me? What would a perfect day in my life look like if I had the connections I wanted? Rather than just, “Well you should reach out more. You should be more connected." Why? To what end? I think a lot of guys, that I know anyway, rebel against that because they're not sure like, when you're done, like, when do I know if this works? Just kind of sitting in the discomfort and like, "OK, am I social now?" Like, "Am I human now?" It just feels too fuzzy. So maybe the first thing they need to do is get it clear in here so that they have a sense of agency. When they're asked to go do something, they can go, "That's not really what I'm looking for" and mean it as opposed to, “Oh, do that.” Like, “My goal is to make this change in my life that would look this way and that doesn't seem like it meets this goal so I'm going to pass." A little more actively than just being kind of like, blown sideways through. "You should be more social for socializing sake," you know what I mean?

BM: Yeah, I mean, I was thinking of it just like a very practical tip. If someone is lonely and they don't know how to talk to another man, I think the easiest thing is to invite someone to coffee and ask them about their life. Because I find that if someone is hesitant or scared or doesn't know how to be vulnerable with another man, it's much easier if someone has gone first. But if you really are feeling the need to do that, then by inviting someone to coffee, you know, ideally someone you have been close to before, and just saying, "Hey, I just want to check in," like, "How is everything going in your life?" That guy is most likely going to share and then that will make it easier for then you to share. So I guess I’m going to [answer] this question much more practical [than] someone watching this right now. They’re like, “Man, I feel like I don’t have any good guy friends anymore. I don't feel like I'm connected to my buddies at all." And actually, I have a short little story about this, which is interesting. I was on my way home for Thanksgiving and I went home, and I was at the time -- gosh, it was 19 years ago. So I was like 29, 30 years old. And I said, "Dad, after Thanksgiving, can we go into the study and I want to interview you about your life." My dad was like, "OK," we were close. And so I asked my dad all these questions about his life, and it was just a great experience. But at the end, I asked him that final question. I said, "Dad, [do] you have any regrets?" And he said, "Blake, I do have one regret." I said, "OK, what is it?" He said, "Look, your mom and I have had this beautiful marriage for now, 37 years. You, your sister and your brother have turned out great. You're all doing different things and following your passion. I've loved my medical practice and helping people. But over the years, I really lost touch with all my guy friends. You know, all my friends from college, all my friends from medical school. You know, I always just said no to the weekend golf guys trips or to this or that, because I was just so busy with you and your mom and my work. And now you guys are in college or out of the house. You know, I'm now getting close to retirement. And I love your mom, but I can't spend every moment with her. And so I don't really have anyone to hang out with. And I'm lonely." And he said, "So don't make that mistake." And so at that time, I was 30 years old. I had just started Toms Shoes -- we were like two years old. And I wrote an email to my seven best friends -- a couple of them from college, some were newer friends in LA -- and I told them the story, and I said, "We can't have this happen to us. Let's do an annual trip every year." And so we started our first trip 19 years ago, and we're getting ready to have our 20th anniversary.
JJ: Where was the first trip?

BM: The first trip was a camping and fishing trip in Colorado. And we've done one trip every single year for 19 years. The group is now 14 guys. We call it the “Rugged Adventure Club.” It was rugged, and then when I sold Toms, it became not so rugged. We started going to the Maldives and all these places.
JJ: You can't call it like, "the guys who glamp," it doesn't ring.

BM: Exactly. But I bring that up because, you know, that group has taught me how to have really meaningful, deep relationships with men, which has had probably as big of an impact on my mental health as anything else.
JJ: I love that story because your dad had the presence of mind and the willingness to be vulnerable with his regrets. Can I tell you my version of that story?
BM: Sure, I'm here for it.

JJ: My father, you know, my father passed away last year and was ill for a very long time. His health declined, declined, declined, declined for years. And he and I were really quite estranged. You know, he and my mother divorced when I was five, the estrangement deepened after I came out. And so it was just kind of like a process. And my father was a Jehovah's Witness, so it was just one thing after another. Eventually I kind of felt convicted and I was like, I need to keep trying to reach out. And I tried to reach out and tried to reach out. Finally, kind of in the last year of his life, he was really not doing well. And I thought, I need to make time to fly home to Florida and just sit down and talk to the guy. And I said, "Dad, I want to do your oral history. I feel like I don't know you. Like, not really know you." Made a special trip, planned the whole thing. "Dad, are we still going to do this?" "Yup, I'll see you in three days." I flew down, checked in the hotel, got up the next day, went to visit my mom, "Dad, are we still on?" "Yep, I'll see you." Another day: "Dad?" "Yep." "Tomorrow. Do it." The morning comes and I call him. "OK, dad. I'm ready to go. When should I come meet you?" "You know ... We've got time. I don't want you to put yourself out and, like, I'm not really feeling up to it. Well don’t worry about it, but we’ve got time.” It's like, "Dad, I booked a flight for you. I bought equipment. I'm ready to do this now." "You know what? Next time you come down, let me know."
BM: Oh, no.
JJ: "We'll do it then, we've got time."
BM: Oh, no.

JJ: And in that moment, I decided, I'm done. I'm not going to ask anymore. I don't know what it was, but I think my father was unable to really process being a dad beyond being a provider. And that human connection of like, "this is how to be a man, this is how to be a Black man," never quite clicked for him, even after I became a storyteller. He knew I was a journalist, very proud of my work, but couldn’t quite get [that] I don’t need what you can provide for me. I need you. And when he passed, I was supposed to like, write his obit. Still haven't. Because I don't know what to write.
BM: OK, so this question is great. I'm assuming it's the one we're already having, but you tell me, what's the most transformational conversation you've ever had?

JJ: Oh, God, I had so many. I mean, I was an interviewer for a living, so I've had way too many. I think the biggest collection of transformational conversations I ever had was when I was a national host on NPR. I got to interview Eric Holder, the former US Attorney General under Barack Obama. And I was really excited to interview him because it was one of the first people of his echelon that I had ever talked to. I was really excited. And then after a while, I could kind of hear my goofy family in the background because we're not highfalutin, we're not fancy people, very together, but we don’t put on airs and attitudes and something about it felt weird. Especially because I wasn't thinking anything about the guest after him. It was nobody famous. And so I decided to like, OK, I'm just going to talk to him like he's any other guest. Invite him in, "How's it going? Have a seat." Make comfortable, very personable guy. Easy to talk to. Segment starts. Break comes. His assistant comes in to remind him, "Sir, we're going to leave halfway through the next segment." We're going to play music and he was going to be able to slip out of the studio. He looks over his shoulder at his assistant and is like, "I think we can stay a few more minutes." Extended the interview on the spot because he was having a good time.
BM: Yeah, yeah.

JJ: And I was, you know, smelling myself for a second, like, "That's right, I'd extended it with me too." But then after it was over, I thought like, dang, I made the right choice. And from that, I kind of reframed the way that I deal with just about everybody. I mean, if you were going to treat every person you will ever meet for the rest of your life exactly the same, how would you treat them? That's what that taught me. Is to be one person, to set one standard, raise or lower, some people you're going to embrace, and some people are going to drive you up the wall. But it sort of made every interview that followed easier because I didn't have to calibrate myself. It’s like conversation no longer depended on anything around me. It depended on everything within me. Like I know who I am as a person, I know what my values are, I know how I want to be treated. That rule is golden for a reason. And I decided that's who I'm going to be. And if we don't vibe, that's cool. If we do, that's fine. But it just made life so much easier and it made the work easier. Like, this is me. Oh, we don't click? OK, cool, that's cool. You get to be you, I get to be me. And we figure it out somewhere along the way. And through all of the ups and downs of talking to all kinds of different people, that was just like, it just greased the wheels for the next three years of that work. It was ... I'm amazed I thought of it. I didn't know I was that bright. I'm glad I had that burst of insight because it made life so much simpler, so much simpler.

BM: I love that, I love that. OK, so for me, what's the most transformational conversation you've ever had? It actually happened about a year ago, with my kids. And I have an 11-year-old and an eight-year-old. And also a 31-year-old adopted son. But this was with the biological kids. And they had seen, you know, and experienced me having a really hard mental health crisis for about two years. I was in and out of treatment centers, I wasn't able to kind of, be there for them in the way that I was before, it was a really hard time. And then I started feeling better. I had some amazing healing experiences, especially around this core wound of not feeling enough. And as I started feeling better, they could tell it was really different. And now I'm spending a lot more time with them. And the conversation I had with them is one day, my son said something about like, "What's different?" And kind of like, well, "How do we know you're not going to feel bad again" type thing? He was worried. I said, “Because now I know that I’m enough, just as I am." Not because of what I've done, not because of what I built, not because of what everyone thinks of me, but just because I exist. And now that I know that, I think my life will always be different. And I saw him like, look. And it was the coolest thing because I then continued the conversation like, "And that extends to you and your sister too. You guys are enough exactly as you are. You can try out for the water polo team, you can try to make good grades, You can try to do these things. But none of that is tied to your worth. I love you, and your mom loves you and the world loves you. And they always will just because you exist." And ever since then, I've seen a lightness in my kids and a connection in us that is so deep, so peaceful, so much that at dinner every night we have this little ritual where we hold hands and my eight-year-old, we start with the youngest first, and she says, "I am enough," and looks around and then she looks at us, she goes, "You are enough," and she goes, "And we are enough." And then the next child does it, and then I do it. And that all came from that conversation. And I hadn't even thought about that until this. But it was one of probably the most important conversations of my life.

JJ: Two questions I have to ask on that. When you said you saw a lightness in your kid, was there anything in particular that you were concerned about getting heavy for them? Like, were there certain aspects of growing up that you thought they needed that message for?

BM: I think when someone does not feel enough, which I didn't for 48 years of my life, then I think you subconsciously project that onto others and especially parents to kids. So if a parent doesn't feel enough and doesn't have their own sense of worth outside of their accomplishments, then you're projecting that pressure onto the kids. So I think my son was feeling like he had to become a great water polo player, or had to be the star of the basketball team, or had to make great grades, or had to look a certain way because I felt that about myself. I never said that to him.
JJ: You don't have to say it.

BM: I didn't have to say it. But as soon as I felt that I was enough and I said that to them, then I saw him reduce the pressure he was putting on himself. And my daughter still, I think, has somewhere to grow in that, because I still think she puts a lot of pressure on herself still. I mean, she's only eight. But I have seen that when we do the ritual at dinner, there's like a twinkle in their eye, there's a smile, there's like, "Yeah, I am enough." And it's a practice. It's not something like, oh, I experienced it once and now I have it forever. It's something that you have to continue to practice every day. You know, that's why I wear the bracelet. It's my reminder every day to go back to this centering. But that conversation with the kids, I think will be one that I'm willing to bet any amount of money if they're sitting in these chairs someday, at least my son would say that was probably the most meaningful conversation.
JJ: I see you have two of those bracelets, and I feel like when you said enough --
BM: You know why I have two?
JJ: Why?

BM: You'll see. So one of my favorite things to do, it's not about wearing it yourself. It's about giving it to someone else. So I always wear an extra one. So if I ever feel like, OK, this is something I want to share with someone, which I do right now, I can give it. So hold out your hand, palm up. There you go. And it says "you are enough" on the inside.
JJ: Oh, wow.
BM: And then ... Now you have one, too.
JJ: I love it, thank you.
BM: You're welcome.
JJ: Thank you so much. When I saw this, I kind of saw this with a period and also with an exclamation point.
BM: It can be both.
JJ: Like, enough! As sort of a check point.
BM: Boundary.
JJ: Or enough, like a relief almost.

BM: It's interesting you bring that up because I originally made it, we hand-make them, these women in India make them. And that's where I had a bunch of my healing. And originally, it was more the "I am enough," a softness. But I also think in the climate that we live in today, there is something also that's a real activist spirit. So it's like, enough! And almost even like, I think of, you know, people who sometimes have been told [in] their life that they're not smart enough or pretty enough or that they're going to amount to enough. It's almost like a "fuck you" to all the people who said you couldn't do it, that you are enough and you don't need their validation.
JJ: I love it. Thank you for this.
BM: OK, let's see. Where did that go?
JJ: Right. It's the daily double. No. If you could redesign how people connect with each other, where would you start?
BM: If I could --
JJ: Wait. You went somewhere. Where did you go?
BM: This is exactly where I went. I went to "Avatar."
JJ: I knew there was something specific.
BM: And Pandora. And if you've watched "Avatar," when the Avatar gets on the horse, then they plug in the hair --
JJ: Yeah.
BM: So that's where I went.
JJ: Where they kind of like --

BM: Yeah. And then I was like, if I could design any way to connect, there'd be some way that like, when we shook hands, I transferred part of my consciousness to you. And so we connected in a nonverbal way. And we could have conversation through touch without having to use our words. That's where I just went.

JJ: But, you know, I get it. I knew you saw something specific. I could see your eyes moving behind your eyebrows. If I could redesign how people connect, I would make it an educational prerequisite. I would put it into schools because that's within our power. I would put listening, communication, and critical thinking as a high school graduation requirement.
BM: Yeah, beautiful.
